Every part of a neural network is something the course has already met: weighted sums
like those of linear regression, each followed by a bend, with weights learned by the
same walk downhill as in [Gradient descent](../04-how-algorithms-learn/gradient-descent.qmd).
The section builds a small network in base R, checks it against arithmetic, then trains
one with tidymodels on the simulated survey. The first two pages open the network up:

- **neurons, layers and activations**: one neuron with no bend is linear regression,
  and two hidden units with opposing bends follow the temperature optimum without being
  told its shape;
- **forward propagation and backpropagation**: a forward pass computes the prediction
  and a backward pass gives every weight its slope, which small nudges of each weight
  confirm.

The next two cover training:

- **training a network**: the learning rate, when to stop and the random start each
  change the result, and the validation error shows how to set them;
- **how much data a network needs**: learning curves compare the network with linear
  regression and a random forest as the survey grows, and the expected counts show that
  the network is short of signal rather than of rows.

The last two show where networks lead:

- **when a network is the right tool**: a water mass forms a diagonal band in
  temperature and salinity, a combination nobody has named, and the network draws it
  from a few hundred stations;
- **autoencoders**: a network that rebuilds its own input through a narrow middle finds
  the plane that principal component analysis finds, with no response to predict.

The section picks up threads from earlier ones.
[Neurons, layers and activations](what-a-network-is.qmd) starts from
[Linear and polynomial regression](../03-supervised-learning/linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd),
and [Forward propagation and backpropagation](forward-and-backward.qmd) applies
[Gradient descent](../04-how-algorithms-learn/gradient-descent.qmd) to every weight at
once. [Training a network](training-a-network.qmd) sets its settings on validation data,
as [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd) does,
and finds that stopping early restrains the weights as
[Regularisation](../05-generalisation/regularisation.qmd) does.
[How much data a network needs](how-much-data.qmd) and
[When a network is the right tool](when-to-use-one.qmd) compare the network with the
forest of [Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd),
and [Autoencoders](autoencoders.qmd) sets a network beside
[Principal component analysis](../08-unsupervised-learning/principal-component-analysis.qmd).

## Further resources

**Documentation**

- [`mlp()`](https://parsnip.tidymodels.org/reference/mlp.html), parsnip. The multilayer perceptron in the same specification idiom as every other model in the course.
- [Neural network models (supervised)](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/neural_networks_supervised.html), scikit-learn user guide. Includes the tips section on scaling and on how little data these need before they overfit.
